lessons.title: Sampling and preparing for quality tests
lessons.html:
The role of quality control

Quality controllers (QCs) test fruit to make sure it meets the standards of the market it is packed for. Tests are done on fruit arriving from the orchard (intake), on the packing line, on packed cartons and on stored fruit. Results guide decisions: whether fruit is mature enough to pick or pack, which market it can go to, and whether storage is working.

Representative sampling

You cannot test every fruit, so you test a sample. The sample must represent the whole batch.

  • Follow the sampling plan for the fruit kind and test: how many fruit, from how many bins or cartons, and how often.
  • Take fruit from different bins, different positions in the bin (top, middle, bottom where possible), and different times in the run.
  • Do not select only the best or worst fruit.
  • Label each sample clearly with producer, orchard or block, cultivar, date, time and batch or pallet number.

Instruments

InstrumentMeasures
Size ring / caliperFruit diameter
ScaleFruit and carton weight
Penetrometer (pressure tester)Flesh firmness
RefractometerTotal soluble solids (TSS, sugar) in degrees Brix
Titration equipmentAcid content
Colour chartsPeel or background colour
Iodine solution and chartStarch breakdown in apples and pears
Thermometer / pulp probeFruit temperature

Calibration

Results are only reliable if instruments are accurate. Zero the refractometer with distilled water before use, check scales with test weights, and check penetrometers as the procedure requires. Record calibration checks. Report and remove any instrument that does not calibrate.

lessons.title: Doing the tests and reporting results
lessons.html:
Typical test procedures

Always follow your packhouse's written method; the outline below shows the main principles.

Firmness

  1. Remove a thin disc of skin on opposite sides of the fruit (usually the cheeks), as the method specifies.
  2. Use the correct plunger tip size for the fruit kind.
  3. Press the penetrometer straight into the flesh at a steady speed to the marked depth.
  4. Read and record the value. Test the set number of fruit and calculate the average.

Sugar (TSS)

  1. Zero the refractometer with distilled water.
  2. Squeeze juice from the fruit, or from a combined sample, onto the prism.
  3. Read the Brix value, record it, and clean and dry the prism.

Acid and juice (citrus)

Juice is extracted, weighed against fruit weight to give juice percentage, and acid is measured by titration. The sugar-acid ratio is then calculated. Handle titration chemicals with gloves and goggles.

Starch (apples and pears)

Cut the fruit across the middle, dip or spray the cut surface with iodine solution, wait the set time, and compare the stain pattern with the starch chart.

External and internal defects

Inspect the sample for blemishes, bruises, sunburn, insect damage and decay, and cut fruit open for internal browning, mealiness, or other internal disorders. Count and classify defects according to the market standard.

Recording and reporting

  • Record results on the QC form or system immediately, with sample details, your name and time.
  • Calculate averages and percentages correctly; double-check calculations.
  • Compare results with the market specification.
  • If results are out of specification, report to the QC supervisor or packhouse manager immediately so the batch can be held, re-graded or redirected. Do not adjust figures.

Safety and hygiene

Use sharp knives carefully, cutting away from yourself on a board. Keep the lab clean, dispose of tested fruit as waste, never return it to the line, and store chemicals labelled and locked.

Key points

  • Take representative samples according to the sampling plan and label them.
  • Calibrate instruments before testing and record it.
  • Use penetrometers, refractometers, titration and iodine tests per method.
  • Record results accurately and compare with the specification.
  • Report out-of-specification results immediately and never change figures.
